profile.behavior: Shy and often concealed; forages quietly on the ground or low in vegetation, taking invertebrates with quick pecks and eating fruit both on the ground and in trees. Males sing from low trees or shrubs, especially around dawn and dusk.
field_marks: Compact, medium-sized thrush with a round head, short straight bill, and relatively long wings
Plain cool-gray face with gray lores and only a faint, incomplete eye ring
Olive-gray to gray-brown upperparts, wings, and tail, without a contrasting rufous tail
Dark spots or stippling across the throat sides and upper breast
Pinkish legs and a slender dark bill with yellowish color at the lower-bill base
profile.habitat: Breeds in dense willow or alder thickets and well-developed understory within boreal coniferous or mixed woodland, especially near the forest–tundra transition. During migration and winter it uses varied forests, second growth, thickets, plantations, and other sites with dense understory or fruiting shrubs.

findings: The primary specimen is a convincing Gray-cheeked Thrush: compact rounded head, short straight bill, long folded wings, plain grayish face, gray lores, subdued eye-ring, gray-brown upperparts, whitish underparts with gray flanks, dark throat and breast spotting, pinkish legs, and no contrasting rufous tail.

The main bird has one head, one beak, one tail, two plausibly attached legs with intact grasping feet, and an anatomically credible pair of wings with the far wing naturally occluded by the side-on pose.
The detached wing and bill/head illustrations are clearly intentional supplementary studies. Both are anatomically coherent and do not appear attached to the primary specimen.

The eye-ring is slightly more visible in the artwork than in some reference photographs, but remains subdued enough to fit documented individual variation and is not rendered as the bold buff spectacle characteristic of Swainson's Thrush.
All visible identification, habitat, behavior, and field-mark text is coherent, correctly spelled, and consistent with the proposed profile and direct-source descriptions.

The stated measurements—length 6.3–6.7 in (16–17 cm), weight 0.9–1.1 oz (26–30 g), and wingspan 12.6–13.4 in (32–34 cm)—faithfully reproduce the directly supported All About Birds measurement set. Audubon's different supported measurement set does not invalidate this compatible single-source set.

The vertical measurement diagram correctly places 6.3 in / 16 cm at the bottom and 6.7 in / 17 cm at the top. Its values increase upward, match the printed length range, and the plate explicitly labels the presentation “SCHEMATIC — NOT TO SCALE.”
The repeated BODY LENGTH line agrees with the main measurement block and ruler endpoints.
No place name, ZIP code, coordinates, map, or local-observation detail appears.
